claim: Over 20 endogenous opioids have been identified.
source: Over 20 endogenous opioids have been identified, all of which preferentially activate one of three opioid receptors – delta, kappa, and mu opioid receptors – which are all members of the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) family of proteins (Gendron et al., 2016; Chavkin, 2013; Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published works (Gendron et al., 2016; Chavkin, 2013; Williams et al., 2013).

claim: Endogenous opioids preferentially activate one of three opioid receptors: delta, kappa, and mu opioid receptors.
source: Over 20 endogenous opioids have been identified, all of which preferentially activate one of three opioid receptors – delta, kappa, and mu opioid receptors – which are all members of the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) family of proteins (Gendron et al., 2016; Chavkin, 2013; Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published works (Gendron et al., 2016; Chavkin, 2013; Williams et al., 2013).

claim: Delta, kappa, and mu opioid receptors are all members of the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) family of proteins.
source: Over 20 endogenous opioids have been identified, all of which preferentially activate one of three opioid receptors – delta, kappa, and mu opioid receptors – which are all members of the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) family of proteins (Gendron et al., 2016; Chavkin, 2013; Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published works (Gendron et al., 2016; Chavkin, 2013; Williams et al., 2013) and draws from established scientific knowledge about receptor classification.

claim: All opioid peptides activate their cognate GPCRs broadly at similar levels in most readouts used to measure activation.
source: All these opioid peptides activate their cognate GPCRs broadly at similar levels in most of the readouts that have been used to measure activation (Sternini et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sternini et al., 2013.

claim: GPCRs are active in endosomes and other intracellular compartments.
source: While this is still an emerging field, a growing body of evidence suggests that GPCRs are active in endosomes and other intracellular compartments, and that receptors in endosomes can cause distinct signaling outcomes compared to receptors on the cell surface (Vilardaga et al., 2014; Bowman et al., 2016; Stoeber et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published works (Vilardaga et al., 2014; Bowman et al., 2016; Stoeber et al., 2018).

claim: Receptors in endosomes can cause distinct signaling outcomes compared to receptors on the cell surface.
source: While this is still an emerging field, a growing body of evidence suggests that GPCRs are active in endosomes and other intracellular compartments, and that receptors in endosomes can cause distinct signaling outcomes compared to receptors on the cell surface (Vilardaga et al., 2014; Bowman et al., 2016; Stoeber et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published works (Vilardaga et al., 2014; Bowman et al., 2016; Stoeber et al., 2018).

claim: Dynorphin A17 (Dyn A), Dynorphin A8 (Dyn A8), Dynorphin B (Dyn B), and α-neoendorphin (α-neo) differ mainly in their length and C-terminal peptide sequence.
source: These peptides differ mainly in their length and C-terminal peptide sequence (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A which shows the schematic of the peptide sequences.

claim: Dyn A, Dyn A8, Dyn B, and α-neo bind KOR at relatively comparable affinities in PC-12 cells and CHO cells.
source: Consistent with previous findings, we find that in these cells Dyn A, Dyn A8, Dyn B, and ɑ-neo bind KOR at relatively comparable affinities (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental binding data presented in Table 1.

claim: Dyn A8, Dyn A, Dyn B, and α-neo (1 μM) inhibit intracellular cAMP levels to a similar extent in PC12 cells stably expressing SpH-KOR.
source: (B) Dyn A8, Dyn A, Dyn B, and α-neo (1 μM) inhibit intracellular cAMP levels to a similar extent in PC12 cells stably expressing SpH-KOR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Dyn A8, Dyn A, Dyn B, and α-neo (1 μM) show roughly similar agonist-mediated receptor clustering at the cell surface following 1 min treatment.
source: (C) Representative TIR-FM images of PC12 cells stably expressing SpH-KOR treated with Dyn A8, Dyn A, Dyn B, and α-neo (1 μM) show roughly similar agonist-mediated receptor clustering at the cell surface following 1 min treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dyn A8, Dyn A, Dyn B, and α-neo (1 μM) induce similar levels of KOR internalization after 5 min of treatment.
source: (D) Quantitation of the loss of surface SpH-KOR fluorescence, as an index of internalization, after 5 min of treatment with each peptide (1 μM), normalized to surface fluorescence before agonist treatment, show similar levels of internalization for all four peptides (mean ± SEM shown, Dyn A: n = 10 cells; Dyn B: n = 10 cells; Dyn A8: n = 10 cells; ɑ-neo: n = 11 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data quantitating surface fluorescence loss shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Dyn A and Dyn B show maximal inhibition of cAMP at approximately 1 μM concentration in SpH-KOR cells.
source: Dose–response curves with Dyn A and Dyn B in SpH-KOR cells showed maximal inhibition ~1 µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental dose-response data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Dyn A and Dyn B endocytose KOR to a similar extent in SpH-KOR cells and CHO-KOR cells.
source: Measurement of cell surface levels of KOR by ELISA show that Dyn A and Dyn B endocytose the receptor to a similar extent in SpH-KOR cells and in CHO-KOR cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C; Gupta et al., 2016), with maximal endocytosis at ~1 µM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C, and by citation to Gupta et al., 2016.

claim: Dyn A and Dyn B show maximal endocytosis of KOR at approximately 1 μM concentration.
source: Measurement of cell surface levels of KOR by ELISA show that Dyn A and Dyn B endocytose the receptor to a similar extent in SpH-KOR cells and in CHO-KOR cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C; Gupta et al., 2016), with maximal endocytosis at ~1 µM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: A significantly higher number of SpH-KOR recycling events was observed 5 min after Dyn B-induced KOR internalization compared to Dyn A, Dyn A8, or α-neo.
source: When the number of SpH-KOR recycling events were quantitated and normalized to time and cell area, a significantly higher number of recycling events was seen 5 min after Dyn B-induced KOR internalization , compared to Dyn A, Dyn A8, or ɑ-neo (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data quantitating recycling events shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SpH-KOR fluorescence is quenched in acidic endosomal compartments and is rapidly dequenched when receptors recycle back to the cell surface.
source: SpH-KOR fluorescence is quenched in acidic endosomal compartments and is rapidly dequenched when receptors recycle back to the cell surface and are exposed to the extracellular media.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about pH-sensitive GFP (SpH) properties.

claim: Dyn B-treated cells showed a higher rate of recovery of surface KOR levels after agonist washout compared to Dyn A at the 30 min time point.
source: When agonist was removed by washing out the media and replacing with fresh media containing antagonist (naltrexone; 10 µm), to specifically measure recycling without the contribution of endocytosis, the fluorescence recovery rate was higher with Dyn B than with Dyn A at the 30 min time point (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fluorescence recovery data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Dyn B showed a higher number of KOR recycling events even in the presence of protease inhibitors.
source: When discrete recycling events were quantitated as in Figure 2D, Dyn B showed a higher number of KOR recycling events even in the presence of protease inhibitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Dyn B-treated cells showed a higher rate of recovery of surface KOR levels after agonist washout compared to Dyn A, even in the presence of protease inhibitors.
source: When the recovery of surface KOR levels after agonist washout were measured by an independent ELISA-based method, Dyn B-treated cells showed a higher rate of recovery compared to Dyn A, even in the presence of protease inhibitors (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ELISA data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Differences in general proteolysis of the peptides did not contribute to the increased KOR recycling observed with Dyn B.
source: These experiments indicate that differences in general proteolysis of the peptides did not contribute to the increased KOR recycling we observe with Dyn B.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that protease inhibitors did not abolish the difference between Dyn A and Dyn B in recycling.

claim: Dyn B, but not Dyn A, can be cleaved by Endothelin Converting Enzyme 2 (ECE2) in vitro.
source: Because Dyn B, but not Dyn A, can be cleaved by Endothelin Converting Enzyme 2 (ECE2) in vitro, we next tested whether this differential proteolysis by ECE2 could contributes to the differences between Dyn A and Dyn B-induced KOR recycling.
evidence: This claim is stated as background knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: S136492 significantly reduced recycling for both Dyn A and Dyn B.
source: S136492 significantly reduced recycling for both Dyn A and Dyn B, indicating that the differences in trafficking between Dyn B and Dyn A cannot be explained solely by ECE2 sensitivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The differences in trafficking between Dyn B and Dyn A cannot be explained solely by ECE2 sensitivity.
source: S136492 significantly reduced recycling for both Dyn A and Dyn B, indicating that the differences in trafficking between Dyn B and Dyn A cannot be explained solely by ECE2 sensitivity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that ECE2 inhibition affected both peptides similarly.

claim: Intrinsic differences between Dyn A and Dyn B contribute to differences in KOR recycling when activated by these peptides.
source: Together, these results suggest that intrinsic differences between Dyn A and Dyn B contribute to differences in KOR recycling when activated by these peptides.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that protease inhibition and ECE2 inhibition did not abolish the differences.

claim: 2 hr treatment with Dyn A caused a loss of 50% of KOR in PC12 cells pretreated with cycloheximide.
source: When total receptor levels were quantified, 2 hr treatment with Dyn A caused a loss of 50% of KOR, while Dyn B treatment caused no loss (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2I and quantified in Figure 2J.

claim: 2 hr treatment with Dyn B caused no loss of KOR in PC12 cells pretreated with cycloheximide.
source: When total receptor levels were quantified, 2 hr treatment with Dyn A caused a loss of 50% of KOR, while Dyn B treatment caused no loss (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2I and quantified in Figure 2J.

claim: After endocytosis, Dyn A preferentially sorts KOR into the degradative pathway, while Dyn B sorts KOR into the recycling pathway.
source: These results suggest that, after endocytosis, Dyn A preferentially sorts KOR into the degradative pathway, while Dyn B sorts KOR into the recycling pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing differential receptor degradation and recycling.

claim: KOR colocalized predominantly with Rab7 when activated by Dyn A in PC12 cells expressing FLAG-KOR and Rab7-GFP.
source: When PC12 cells expressing FLAG-KOR and Rab7-GFP, to mark the late endocytic pathway, were treated with 1 µM Dyn A for 20 min and imaged live, KOR colocalized predominantly with Rab7 (example in Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: KOR localized mainly to compartments marked by Rab7 and Lamp1 when activated by Dyn A.
source: KOR localized mainly to compartments marked by Rab7 and Lamp1 when activated by Dyn A, but to compartments marked by EEA1, Rab5, and Rab11 when activated by Dyn B (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: KOR localized mainly to compartments marked by EEA1, Rab5, and Rab11 when activated by Dyn B.
source: KOR localized mainly to compartments marked by Rab7 and Lamp1 when activated by Dyn A, but to compartments marked by EEA1, Rab5, and Rab11 when activated by Dyn B (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: KOR is concentrated in different endosomal compartments based on the Dynorphin that activates it.
source: These results show that KOR is concentrated in different endosomal compartments based on the Dynorphin that activates it.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing differential colocalization with endosomal markers.

claim: Nb39 localized efficiently to endosomes that contained Dyn A-activated KOR in PC12 cells.
source: A nanobody (Nb39) that specifically recognizes the active conformation of KOR (Che et al., 2018), when co-expressed with FLAG-KOR in PC12 cells, localized efficiently to endosomes that also contained Dyn A-activated KOR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Che et al., 2018.

claim: Nb39 localized less to endosomes containing Dyn B-activated KOR compared to Dyn A-activated KOR.
source: In contrast, Nb39 localized less to endosomes containing Dyn B-activated KOR (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Endosomes containing Dyn A-activated KOR recruited Nb39 at a significantly higher level than those containing Dyn B-activated KOR.
source: When the fraction of total number of KOR endosomes/cell that colocalized with Nb39 was quantitated by analyzing 3D stacks, endosomes containing Dyn A-activated KOR recruited Nb39 at a significantly higher level (Figure 3F and G), suggesting that KOR was in an active conformation in the endosomes specifically after activation by Dyn A.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental quantitation data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: KOR was in an active conformation in the endosomes specifically after activation by Dyn A.
source: When the fraction of total number of KOR endosomes/cell that colocalized with Nb39 was quantitated by analyzing 3D stacks, endosomes containing Dyn A-activated KOR recruited Nb39 at a significantly higher level (Figure 3F and G), suggesting that KOR was in an active conformation in the endosomes specifically after activation by Dyn A.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing Nb39 recruitment to Dyn A-activated KOR endosomes.

claim: Nb39 recruitment to endosomes required KOR endocytosis.
source: Nb39 recruitment to endosomes required KOR endocytosis, as recruitment was abolished when cells were treated with agonist in the presence of 40 µM Dyngo4A, an endocytosis inhibitor (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: In cells treated with 1 μM Dyn A, approximately 15% of all KOR endosomes colocalized with both Nb39 and Lysotracker.
source: When the colocalization was quantitated in Dyn A-treated cells, ~15% of all KOR endosomes colocalized with both markers, suggesting that a subset of Dyn A-activated KOR in the lysosome was in the active conformation (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental quantitation data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: A subset of Dyn A-activated KOR in the lysosome was in the active conformation.
source: When the colocalization was quantitated in Dyn A-treated cells, ~15% of all KOR endosomes colocalized with both markers, suggesting that a subset of Dyn A-activated KOR in the lysosome was in the active conformation (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing colocalization of KOR with Nb39 and Lysotracker.

claim: In cells treated with 1 μM Dyn B, virtually no KOR endosomes colocalized with both Nb39 and Lysotracker.
source: In cells treated with 1 µM Dyn B, however, virtually no KOR endosomes colocalized with both Nb39 and Lysotracker (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Twenty-five minutes after agonist washout, Dyn A-activated KOR was still localized predominantly to Rab7-labeled late endosomal compartments.
source: Twenty-five minutes after agonist washout, Dyn A-activated KOR was still localized predominantly to Rab7-labeled late endosomal compartments, while Dyn B-activated KOR was localized predominantly to Rab11-labeled recycling endosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–H.

claim: Twenty-five minutes after agonist washout, Dyn B-activated KOR was localized predominantly to Rab11-labeled recycling endosomes.
source: Twenty-five minutes after agonist washout, Dyn A-activated KOR was still localized predominantly to Rab7-labeled late endosomal compartments, while Dyn B-activated KOR was localized predominantly to Rab11-labeled recycling endosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–H.

claim: Dyn A, but not Dyn B, caused sustained decrease in cAMP levels under conditions where the majority of KOR was in late endosomes and lysosomes.
source: Strikingly, Dyn A, but not Dyn B, caused sustained decrease in cAMP levels under conditions where the majority of KOR was in late endosomes and lysosomes (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental cAMP measurement data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Dyn A, but not Dyn B, specifically coordinates activation and cAMP inhibition by KOR in late endosomes and lysosomes.
source: Together, our results suggest that Dyn A, but not Dyn B, specifically coordinates activation and cAMP inhibition by KOR in late endosomes and lysosomes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing sustained cAMP inhibition by Dyn A when KOR is in late endosomes and lysosomes.

claim: Dynorphin-selective coordination of KOR recycling and endosomal activation was conserved in striatal neurons.
source: Importantly, this Dynorphin-selective coordination of KOR recycling and endosomal activation was conserved in striatal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from striatal neurons shown in Figure 4.

claim: The number of individual exocytic events was significantly lower in neurons treated for 30 min with 1 μM Dyn A compared to Dyn B.
source: The number of individual exocytic events, when quantified per minute and normalized to cell area, was significantly lower in neurons treated for 30 min with 1 µM Dyn A compared to Dyn B (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental quantitation data from neurons shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Dyn B, but not Dyn A, preferentially sorted KOR to recycling endosomes in neurons.
source: This suggested that Dyn B, but not Dyn A, preferentially sorted KOR to recycling endosomes in neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing differential recycling rates in neurons.

claim: KOR colocalized predominantly with Rab7 when activated by Dyn A in striatal neurons.
source: KOR colocalized predominantly with Rab7 when activated by Dyn A, and with Rab11 when activated by Dyn B (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental colocalization data from neurons shown in Figure 4B.

claim: KOR colocalized predominantly with Rab11 when activated by Dyn B in striatal neurons.
source: KOR colocalized predominantly with Rab7 when activated by Dyn A, and with Rab11 when activated by Dyn B (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental colocalization data from neurons shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Endosomes containing Dyn A-activated KOR recruited Nb33 in neurons.
source: Endosomes containing Dyn A-activated KOR recruited Nb33, while endosomes containing Dyn B-activated KOR recruited Nb33 to a noticeably lesser extent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from neurons.

claim: Endosomes containing Dyn B-activated KOR recruited Nb33 to a noticeably lesser extent than Dyn A-activated KOR in neurons.
source: Endosomes containing Dyn A-activated KOR recruited Nb33, while endosomes containing Dyn B-activated KOR recruited Nb33 to a noticeably lesser extent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from neurons.

claim: The percentage of KOR endosomes that recruited Nb33 was significantly higher for Dyn A-activated KOR than for Dyn B in neurons.
source: The percentage of KOR endosomes that recruited Nb33 was significantly higher for Dyn A-activated KOR than for Dyn B (Figure 4E), showing that dynorphin-selective spatial activation of KOR was conserved in neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental quantitation data from neurons shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Dynorphin-selective spatial activation of KOR was conserved in neurons.
source: The percentage of KOR endosomes that recruited Nb33 was significantly higher for Dyn A-activated KOR than for Dyn B (Figure 4E), showing that dynorphin-selective spatial activation of KOR was conserved in neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing differential Nb33 recruitment in neurons.

claim: Two related peptides, Dynorphin A and Dynorphin B, bind and activate KOR to similar extents in mammalian neuroendocrine cells and rat striatal neurons.
source: We show that two related peptides, Dynorphin A and Dynorphin B, bind and activate KOR to similar extents in mammalian neuroendocrine cells and rat striatal neurons, but localize KOR to distinct intracellular compartments and drive different post-endocytic fates of the receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Dynorphin A and Dynorphin B localize KOR to distinct intracellular compartments.
source: We show that two related peptides, Dynorphin A and Dynorphin B, bind and activate KOR to similar extents in mammalian neuroendocrine cells and rat striatal neurons, but localize KOR to distinct intracellular compartments and drive different post-endocytic fates of the receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential colocalization with endosomal markers.

claim: Dynorphin A and Dynorphin B drive different post-endocytic fates of KOR.
source: We show that two related peptides, Dynorphin A and Dynorphin B, bind and activate KOR to similar extents in mammalian neuroendocrine cells and rat striatal neurons, but localize KOR to distinct intracellular compartments and drive different post-endocytic fates of the receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential recycling and degradation.

claim: Localization of KOR to the degradative pathway by Dynorphin A induces sustained KOR signaling from these compartments.
source: Strikingly, localization of KOR to the degradative pathway by Dynorphin A induces sustained KOR signaling from these compartments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing sustained cAMP inhibition by Dyn A when KOR is in late endosomes and lysosomes.

claim: Seemingly redundant endogenous peptides can fine-tune signaling by regulating the spatiotemporal profile of KOR signaling.
source: Our results suggest that seemingly redundant endogenous peptides can fine-tune signaling by regulating the spatiotemporal profile of KOR signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing differential spatial and temporal signaling patterns.

claim: Dyn A and Dyn B are processed from adjacent regions of pro-dynorphin.
source: We focused on Dyn A and Dyn B as a highly relevant and interesting pair, as both are processed from adjacent regions of pro-dynorphin and are often co-expressed in physiologically relevant brain regions (Nikoshkov et al., 2005; Corder et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A showing the schematic of pro-dynorphin and citations to Nikoshkov et al., 2005 and Corder et al., 2018.

claim: Dyn A and Dyn B are often co-expressed in physiologically relevant brain regions.
source: We focused on Dyn A and Dyn B as a highly relevant and interesting pair, as both are processed from adjacent regions of pro-dynorphin and are often co-expressed in physiologically relevant brain regions (Nikoshkov et al., 2005; Corder et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nikoshkov et al., 2005 and Corder et al., 2018.

claim: Peptidases localized to endosomes, like endothelin-converting enzymes (ECEs), may provide another level of regulation for agonist-dependent KOR trafficking.
source: Peptidases localized to endosomes, like endothelin-converting enzymes (ECEs) may provide another level of regulation for agonist-dependent KOR trafficking (Padilla et al., 2007; Roosterman et al., 2007; Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Padilla et al., 2007; Roosterman et al., 2007; Gupta et al., 2015.

claim: ECE peptide-sensitivity is not the only or primary factor that determines agonist-dependent KOR localization.
source: However, our results do not suggest that ECE peptide-sensitivity is the only or primary factor that determines agonist-dependent KOR localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that ECE2 inhibition did not abolish the differences between Dyn A and Dyn B.

claim: Ubiquitination of KOR may regulate its ability to traffic to and signal from late endosomal and lysosomal compartments.
source: Ubiquitination of KOR may also regulate its ability to traffic to and signal from late endosomal and lysosomal compartments (Li et al., 2008; Henry et al., 2011; Dores and Trejo, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2008; Henry et al., 2011; Dores and Trejo, 2019.

claim: KOR sorting probably involves interactions with PDZ-interacting protein NHERF1/EBP50.
source: Because the post-endocytic sorting of GPCRs is usually mediated by specific interactions of the unstructured cytoplasmic tail of the receptors with trafficking proteins, KOR sorting probably involves interactions with PDZ-interacting protein NHERF1/EBP50 (Liu-Chen, 2004).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from general GPCR sorting mechanisms and citation to Liu-Chen, 2004.

claim: Different Dynorphin peptides could lock KOR into conformations that selectively allow or inhibit interactions with trafficking and signaling proteins.
source: In this context, different Dynorphin peptides could lock KOR into conformations that selectively allow or inhibit interactions with trafficking and signaling proteins, essentially defining the receptor interactome in an agonist-specific manner.
evidence: This claim is speculative about the mechanism underlying the observed differences.

claim: Different Dynorphins could cause agonist-specific post-translational modifications.
source: It is possible that different Dynorphins could cause agonist-specific post-translational modifications, which is a general emerging theme for opioid receptors (Chiu et al., 2017; Mann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to Chiu et al., 2017 and Mann et al., 2019.

claim: Mu opioid receptor can exist in an active conformation in earlier endosomal compartments.
source: For example, other Gi-coupled receptors such as the mu opioid receptor can exist in an active conformation in earlier endosomal compartments (Stoeber et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stoeber et al., 2018.

claim: Internalization is required for sustained inhibition of cAMP for many receptors, such as for the class B S1P receptor.
source: Internalization is required for sustained inhibition of cAMP for many receptors, such as for the class B S1P receptor (Willinger et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Willinger et al., 2014.

claim: Gi is likely present on late endosomal and lysosomal compartments.
source: However, Gi is likely present on late endosomal and lysosomal compartments, as cannabinoid receptors trafficking from the Golgi can activate Gi on lysosomes (Rozenfeld and Devi, 2008).
evidence: This claim is inferred from evidence about cannabinoid receptors and supported by citation to Rozenfeld and Devi, 2008.

claim: The binding of peptides to opioid receptors does not change dramatically at lower pH.
source: Further, the binding of peptides to opioid receptors does not change dramatically at lower pH (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gupta et al., 2015.

claim: Gi could be activated at multiple endosomal compartments based on the specific opioid receptor and ligand, leading to distinct early and late phases of endosomal signaling.
source: Therefore, it is possible that Gi could be activated at multiple endosomal compartments based on the specific opioid receptor and ligand, leading to distinct early and late phases of endosomal signaling.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the experimental results and cited evidence.

claim: Three lysine residues on the C-terminus of KOR are required for normal levels of degradation of KOR, but not for internalization from the surface.
source: For example, three lysine residues on the C-terminus of KOR are required for normal levels of degradation of KOR, but not for internalization from the surface (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2008.

claim: Ubiquitination plays complex roles in receptor trafficking and signaling at the endosome, controlling transport of receptors to lysosomes, entry of receptors into intralumenal vesicles, and recruitment of signaling scaffolds.
source: Ubiquitination, however, plays complex roles in receptor trafficking and signaling at the endosome, controlling transport of receptors to lysosomes, entry of receptors into intralumenal vesicles, and recruitment of signaling scaffolds that could initiate non-canonical signaling pathways (Patwardhan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Patwardhan et al., 2021.

claim: Dyn A-activated KOR could activate alternate pathways, such as mTOR signaling, on late endosomes and lysosomes.
source: In this context, Dyn A-activated KOR could also activate alternate pathways, such as mTOR signaling, on late endosomes and lysosomes.
evidence: This claim is speculative about potential signaling pathways.

claim: mTOR signaling is involved in potentially deleterious effects of KOR.
source: Interestingly, mTOR signaling is involved in potentially deleterious effects of KOR, leading to efforts to generate agonists bypassing this signaling pathway (Che and Roth, 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Che and Roth, 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Under the conditions tested, there was no significant increase in p70S6 phosphorylation upon activation of KOR with either Dyn A or Dyn B.
source: However, under the conditions we tested, we did not see a significant increase in p70S6 phosphorylation, as a readout for mTOR activation, upon activation of KOR with either Dyn A or Dyn B.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: KOR is activated by many opioid peptides that are generated from multiple precursor peptides, some of which bias signaling from the cell surface to different outputs.
source: KOR is activated by many opioid peptides that are generated from multiple precursor peptidesproteins, some of which bias signaling from the cell surface to different outputs (Gomes et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gomes et al., 2020.

claim: The fractions of receptors seen at steady state likely represent an equilibrium of many rounds of rapid iterative sorting as the endosome matures.
source: The fractions of receptors we see at steady state likely represent an equilibrium of many rounds of rapid iterative sorting as the endosome matures, where only a small fraction is recycled back to the surface in the case of Dyn A, while a large fraction is recycled in the case of Dyn B.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and represents an interpretation of the data.

claim: Dyn A drives little KOR to recycle and promotes endosomal KOR activation, causing sustained cAMP inhibition from endosomes after a single exposure.
source: Because Dyn A drives little KOR to recycle and promotes endosomal KOR activation, the net effect would be to cause a sustained cAMP inhibition from endosomes after a single exposure.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing low recycling and sustained signaling with Dyn A.

claim: Dyn B drives KOR recycling and induces endosomal signaling only to small amounts, causing short-lived cAMP inhibition primarily from the surface.
source: Because Dyn B drives KOR recycling and induces endosomal signaling only to small amounts, the net effect would be short-lived cAMP inhibition primarily from the surface.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing high recycling and low endosomal signaling with Dyn B.

claim: The rapid recycling and resensitization caused by Dyn B would sensitize cells to repeated pulses of ligand release, unlike with Dyn A.
source: On the other hand, the rapid recycling and resensitization caused by Dyn B would sensitize cells to repeated pulses of ligand release, unlike with Dyn A.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing differential recycling rates.

claim: Small differences in steady-state localization can cause relevant changes in signaling.
source: This difference in steady-state localization, however, is enough to cause a difference in endosomal receptor activation and cAMP signaling, suggesting that small differences in steady-state localization can cause relevant changes in signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that differential localization correlates with differential signaling.
